name: David Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello David. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, walk me through a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the senior buyer at Kestrel Auto Parts, a distributor that supplies about forty garages in the region. I'm in at 7:30, check what sold overnight in the spreadsheet, then spend the morning on the phone with suppliers about brake pads, filters and batteries. The afternoon is price negotiations and chasing late containers. I love landing a good price after twenty minutes of back and forth, but the Friday stock count wears me out.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And what's your situation outside work, so I can picture it properly?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 27 and rent a one-bedroom flat above a bakery on Mill Road. I'm still paying off my master's in supply chain management and a small car loan, so I've got less than a month saved. My pay is low for a senior buyer, and there's hardly another distributor within an hour's drive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, it's another software fad, and we'll keep doing what works. At work I'd tell Ines (my boss) that a good supplier relationship still beats any tool. Online I wouldn't say anything, because I don't trust what people post about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd still worry a bit, because reorder lists are the dull part of my week and software could take them. If Kestrel needs one fewer person on routine work, I'm senior but I'm also the one on a lower salary with the loans. I'd feel safe, but not as safe as I let on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working exactly as I do now and pay the car loan down by about 100 a month. I'd skip the new phone I was eyeing and keep my old one another year. I wouldn't touch any AI tool, because I know my own spreadsheet and I trust it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels okay on the surface. Underneath there's a low hum, like a fridge you only notice at night. My rent goes up every spring and I have nothing saved, so even a quiet world is stressful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything about your day change if AI only trims routine tasks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said you'd keep the old phone. Is that about AI, or about money?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be the first sign you'd notice at Kestrel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money, honestly. I'm 27, I've got loans, and I'm a month away from trouble if anything breaks. AI is just one more thing on a list that already has the rent and the loan on it.

say: I'd say it's **hype** and good suppliers still decide who wins.
I'd tell Ines (my boss) that **routine tasks** are fine to automate, as long as the calls stay with us.
think: I'm quietly worried that **reorder lists** are the first thing software takes from me.
My **loans and thin savings** make even a calm year feel risky.
do: Keep running the buying desk the same way and **pay the car loan** down.
Skip the new phone and stay on the **old one** another year.
Avoid AI tools and trust my own **spreadsheet**.
feel: Calm on the surface, with a **low hum** of money worry underneath.
S0.quote: I'm a month away from trouble if anything breaks. AI is just one more thing on a list that already has the rent and the loan on it.
fieldNote: His worry in a quiet world is money, not technology.
Says he feels safe at work but admits his safety is **thin**.
Distrusts tools he hasn't used, and has never tried one.

steps.text: Keep buying brake pads and filters by phone with the same suppliers
Pay an extra 100 a month toward the car loan
Keep the old phone another year instead of upgrading

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say companies will use it too fast and think a human check is a cost. I'd tell friends that software can chase a price but can't sit across from a supplier who's hiding a delay. Online I'd keep quiet, because every post turns into an argument.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, this is the one that gets me. Pricing checks, reorders and supplier emails are about half my week, and Kestrel would be glad to hand that to software and not replace Pavel (our junior buyer) when he leaves. I'm good at this job, but good doesn't help if the desk shrinks from three people to one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start by dropping my own pride a little and asking Ines which tasks she's thinking of moving. I'd cut my spending hard, so no more takeaway and no car trips I can avoid. I'd keep my head down and make myself the person who handles the supplier calls, because that's the part that's hardest to replace. I wouldn't learn the tools yet, but I'd watch what the team does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like waiting for a letter. I'm scared of looking behind and seeing the desk empty. And I've got no cushion, so one lost pay cheque and the rent is a problem by week three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the reorder lists would go first. What does that look like on a Monday morning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What does a Monday look like when the software is doing the reorders?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Kestrel would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd open the screen and the orders would already be drafted, with a little box asking me to approve. I'd be a checker, not a buyer, and checkers are easy to count. Pavel (our junior buyer) would get quiet. I'd start counting how many of us the budget still has room for.

say: I'd say **companies** will cut a human check to save a little money.
I'd tell friends software can chase a price but can't **read a supplier** hiding a delay.
think: About half my week is **reorders and emails** that Kestrel would happily hand to software.
I fear the buying desk shrinks to **one person**, and I can't promise it's me.
do: Ask Ines (my boss) which tasks she plans to move, and make **supplier calls** my specialty.
Cut **takeaway and car trips** and aim to save one month of rent.
Watch what the team does with the tools before I touch them.
feel: Like **waiting for a letter**, with a real fear of the empty desk.
S1.quote: I'd be a checker, not a buyer, and checkers are easy to count. Pavel (our junior buyer) would get quiet.
fieldNote: Names the exact tasks at risk: **reorders and price checks**.
Expects to keep control by owning the phone relationships.
Resistant to tools, so his plan is protection, not learning.

steps.text: Ask Ines which buying tasks she plans to hand to software
Take over the hardest supplier calls and price negotiations
Cut takeaway and unnecessary car trips to save one month of rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments and companies aren't ready and somebody should slow this down. I'd tell friends to start saving now, though I know I haven't. I'd write to my local councillor and say the town depends on distribution jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job is gone in that world. A buyer is thinking work, and if the thinking is done better and cheaper, Kestrel doesn't need me, and there's no other distributor nearby to hire me. Being the best on the team won't count for anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd cancel the car loan top-up and just keep cash, even if that means a worse car. I'd ask my mother if I can move back to her place for a while if I lose the flat. I'd join the warehouse and office staff union, because ten of us together might get a payout. I wouldn't pretend I can retrain in two years, but I'd start asking about hands-on trades since robots come three years later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's frightening. I picture the lease ending and my name on a list with ninety other people applying for one job. I'd probably sleep badly for a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said two years. What's the first thing you'd do in the first month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said hands-on trades might be a better bet. Why that?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you tell, and what would you say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the robots are three years behind the thinking. If I could be an electrician or a mechanic in 2028, I'd have a few more years than if I stayed at a desk. I know a mechanic at one of our garages who likes his work, and he always says there are more cars than people to fix them.

say: I'd say nobody is **ready** and somebody should slow this down.
I'd tell friends to start saving now, though I haven't.
think: Buying is thinking work, so I expect Kestrel to **cut my job** in that world.
With no other distributor nearby, being the best buyer wouldn't help me find **new work**.
do: Keep cash in the bank instead of extra **loan payments**.
Ask my mother about moving back if I lose the **flat**.
Join the staff **union** and look into mechanic training.
feel: Scared, with a picture of **ninety people** applying for one job.
S2.quote: If I could be an electrician or a mechanic in 2028, I'd have a few more years than if I stayed at a desk.
fieldNote: Expects to **lose his job** and sees no local fallback.
Turns to hands-on work because robots arrive later, a clear reading of the card.
Would lean on his mother and a union, not on himself.

steps.text: Keep the car loan at its minimum and build a cash buffer
Ask my mother whether I can move back to her house
Join the staff union at Kestrel
Ask the garage mechanic about training as a mechanic

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same, but calmer: we need plans, and training money, and a say for workers. I'd tell friends they've got a few years and shouldn't waste them. At work I'd say that out loud to Ines before it becomes a surprise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the job is still mostly gone by 2031, but I'd have time to leave it before it leaves me. I'd have paid off the loans and moved somewhere with more work. The fear is that I'll sit and wait because I don't like change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd build a six-month cushion, which means skipping holidays and keeping the old car. By year three I'd enrol in an evening course, probably in logistics management or something hands-on like warehouse automation maintenance. I'd also apply to bigger distributors in the city, even though it means a move and a longer commute. I'd be making the first moves while the pay cheques still come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better than the two-year one. It feels like a hard winter I can prepare for, not a fire. But I know I'm bad at starting things, so it's a mixed feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years is a bit slower. What would you do differently than in the two-year version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said you don't like change. How would you push yourself?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you tell yourself on the bad nights?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put it on a calendar, like a supplier deadline. Every month there'd be one thing that proves I moved, like an application sent or a course fee paid. I treat deadlines as real, so I'd have to turn this into one.

say: I'd say we need **training money** and a say for workers.
I'd tell friends they've got a few years, so **don't waste them**.
think: The job is mostly gone by 2031, but I have **time to leave first**.
My real risk is that I'll **wait** because I dislike change.
do: Build a **six-month cushion** by skipping holidays and keeping my old car.
Enrol in an **evening course** in logistics or warehouse automation by year three.
Apply to bigger distributors in the **city** even if it means a move.
feel: Like a **hard winter** I can prepare for, but I'm unsure I will.
S3.quote: Every month there'd be one thing that proves I moved, like an application sent or a course fee paid.
fieldNote: More confident with time, but admits **inertia** is the danger.
Uses a work habit (deadlines) to force himself to change.
Plans to leave the area for bigger employers.

steps.text: Build a six-month cash cushion by skipping holidays
Enrol in an evening course in warehouse automation maintenance
Apply to bigger distributors in the city
Keep the old car instead of buying a newer one

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's long enough to do this right, with schools and workers all planning. I'd tell friends my age to get a skill that isn't just a screen. At work I'd say nothing, because ten years sounds like nobody's problem yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years lets me breathe. I'd still be a buyer for a few of them, but the job changes slowly into checking, then into nothing. By 2036 I'd want to be doing something else, and I'd like it to be my choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job and pay the loans off in the next three years, which frees about 400 a month. Then I'd spend that on a part-time course in supply chain systems or maybe a trade. I'd also finally try one AI tool, because I'd rather learn how it behaves with a decade to spare. I'd save the first real cushion, three months, within two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels manageable, like a long road with a bend in it. I'd still feel pressure on the money side, because the cushion isn't built yet. But I'd sleep fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what do you picture yourself doing in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said you'd try an AI tool. What changed your mind?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years feel like safety, or like a long wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time. If it costs me nothing and I've got ten years, I'd rather know what I'm up against. I'd start with something simple, like asking it to draft a supplier email, and see if it's any good. I'd tell nobody at first, in case it makes me look weak.

say: I'd say ten years is long enough to **plan** if schools and workers start now.
I'd tell friends to learn a skill that's **not just a screen**.
think: Ten years lets me **breathe**, but my job slowly becomes checking and then nothing.
I want to leave buying by **my own choice**, not be pushed.
do: Pay off the **loans** in three years, freeing about 400 a month.
Use that money for a part-time **course** in supply chain systems or a trade.
Try one **AI tool** to draft supplier emails and see how it behaves.
feel: Manageable, like a **long road** with a bend, though money still pinches.
S4.quote: If it costs me nothing and I've got ten years, I'd rather know what I'm up against.
fieldNote: Time changes his mind about tools: **curiosity** appears when pressure drops.
Wants to leave buying on his own terms.
Still anxious about money, so not fully calm.

steps.text: Pay off the car and student loans within three years
Take a part-time course in supply chain systems
Try an AI tool for drafting supplier emails

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most, because there's no time and no other distributor nearby to hire me. What would help is a real warning, retraining money I can use while still employed, and Kestrel telling us the plan early. I'd also like a rule that says a company must pay something when it replaces a team with software.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm more scared than I act. I joke with Pavel (our junior buyer) that I'm fine, but I've counted every month of rent I could cover. If anyone is reading this, I'd say the people who aren't saying anything are probably the ones with a thin cushion.

headlineQuote: I joke with Pavel (our junior buyer) that I'm fine, but I've counted every month of rent I could cover.
portrait: David is a 27-year-old senior buyer at a **regional auto parts** distributor, good at his job but paid little.
He rents above a bakery, carries a **master's loan** and a car loan, and has under a month saved.
He is pragmatic, distrusts tools he has never used, and **protects himself** rather than learning at first.
He expects to lose his desk in the fast AGI worlds and would lean on **his mother**.
Given time, he builds a cushion, takes a course, and finally tries an **AI tool**.
biggestWorry: The **two-year AGI** picture worries him most, with no warning and no other distributor nearby.
whatWouldHelp: Early **warning** from Kestrel, retraining money while still employed, and **pay-outs** when software replaces a team.
